title: OOP Revision Notes: Classes, Objects and the Four Pillars
summary: Night-before revision notes on classes and objects, encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism (overloading vs overriding) and composition vs inheritance. Covers the mental model, how to apply each pillar, the usual mistakes and a closing cheat sheet.

chapters.title: Classes and Objects: The Mental Model
points: A class is a blueprint that defines state (fields) and behavior (methods); an object is one instance of it created at runtime
Each object has its own copy of instance fields, while static members belong to the class and are shared by all instances
A constructor runs on object creation to initialise state; if you define none, the compiler supplies a no-arg default constructor
Example: Car c = new Car("red"); c.drive(); creates one object and calls a method on it through the reference c
Gotcha: a reference is not the object; assigning b = a copies the reference, so both point to the same object and changes show through either

chapters.title: Encapsulation and Abstraction
points: Encapsulation bundles data with the methods that act on it and hides the fields behind private access
Getters and setters let you validate input and change internals without breaking callers
Example: private double balance; public void deposit(double x) { if (x <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException(); balance += x; }
Abstraction exposes what an object does and hides how, via abstract classes and interfaces
Encapsulation vs abstraction: encapsulation protects state (information hiding); abstraction simplifies the design by modelling only essential behavior
Gotcha: a public getter that returns a mutable internal list leaks the state, so return a copy or an unmodifiable view

chapters.title: Inheritance and the super Keyword
points: Inheritance lets a subclass reuse and extend a superclass, modelling an is-a relationship (Dog is an Animal)
Syntax: class Dog extends Animal; the subclass inherits non-private fields and methods
super(...) calls the parent constructor and must be the first statement in the child constructor; super.method() calls the parent version
Java allows single class inheritance only; multiple behavior comes from implementing several interfaces
Abstract class vs interface: an abstract class can hold state and constructors, while an interface defines a contract that many unrelated classes can implement
Gotcha: use final to stop a class from being extended or a method from being overridden

chapters.title: Polymorphism: Overloading vs Overriding
points: Polymorphism means one interface, many forms: the same call behaves differently depending on the object
Overloading: same method name, different parameter lists in the same class, resolved at compile time (static binding)
Overriding: a subclass redefines an inherited method with the same signature, resolved at runtime by the actual object type (dynamic dispatch)
Example: Animal a = new Dog(); a.speak(); runs Dog.speak(), because the runtime type decides, not the reference type
Overloading vs overriding: return type alone cannot overload; an override needs the same signature, a return type that is the same or covariant, and access no narrower than the parent
Gotcha: static, private and final methods cannot be overridden (static methods are hidden); add @Override so the compiler catches typos

chapters.title: Composition vs Inheritance
points: Composition is a has-a relationship: a class holds another object as a field and delegates work to it (Car has an Engine)
Inheritance is a compile-time, tight coupling to the parent, while composition is loose and can be swapped at runtime
Example: class Car { private Engine engine; Car(Engine e) { this.engine = e; } void start() { engine.start(); } }
Rule of thumb: inherit only for a true is-a relationship that keeps the parent's contract; otherwise favour composition
Gotcha: inheriting just to reuse code creates fragile base classes, because a change in the parent can break every child
Gotcha: deep hierarchies are hard to follow, so prefer shallow ones, and combine composition with interfaces for flexibility

chapters.title: OOP Cheat Sheet
points: Class = blueprint, object = instance, static = shared by the class, instance = one copy per object
Encapsulation = private fields + public methods; abstraction = expose what, hide how
Inheritance = is-a, extends, super(); overriding = same signature in the child, runtime; overloading = same name, different parameters, compile time
Polymorphism: the reference type decides what you can call, the object type decides which override runs
Choose is-a for inheritance and has-a for composition; default to composition and use @Override and final deliberately
